explain.title: Real numbers
explain.body: The real numbers are the union of rational numbers and irrational numbers: R = Q ∪ Q'. Rational numbers can be expressed as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Irrational numbers cannot be expressed as a quotient of integers.

explain.title: Decimal types
explain.body: A decimal that ends is terminating. A decimal with a repeating pattern that continues forever is non-terminating and recurring; both types are rational. A decimal that continues forever without repeating is irrational.

explain.title: Recurring decimals as fractions
explain.body: Let the recurring decimal be x. Multiply x by 10 for a one-digit repeating block, or by 100 for a two-digit repeating block. Subtract the original equation to cancel the repeating digits, then solve for x.

explain.title: Properties and inequalities
explain.body: Real-number properties describe how addition and multiplication behave. For inequalities, adding the same number to both sides keeps the inequality direction. Multiplying by a negative number reverses the direction.

explain.title: Numbers between two numbers
explain.body: One way to find a rational number between two numbers is to find their average. Repeating the method with a new pair can give another rational number between the original numbers.

mistakes: Calling every decimal that continues forever irrational: recurring decimals are rational.
Forgetting that a rational number must have a non-zero denominator.
Using 10 instead of 100 when the repeating block has two digits.
Subtracting recurring-decimal equations incorrectly so the repeating parts do not cancel.
Forgetting to reverse an inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Naming a property without specifying whether it is over addition or multiplication when that distinction is needed.

explain.title: Radicals and indices
explain.body: If n is a positive integer greater than 1 and a is a real number, then any real number x such that x = ⁿ√a is called nᵗʰ root of a. Here, √ is called radical and n is the index of radical. A real number under the radical sign is called a radicand. Exponential form of x = ⁿ√a is x = (a)^(1/n).

explain.title: Laws of radicals and indices
explain.body: Use the laws to split products and quotients inside a radical, or to rewrite roots as fractional powers. For example, ⁿ√(ab) = ⁿ√a · ⁿ√b and a^m/a^n = a^(m−n). A negative exponent means take the reciprocal.

explain.title: Surds and conjugates
explain.body: An irrational radical with rational radicand is called a surd. A surd containing one term is a monomial surd; a surd containing the sum of two monomial surds is a binomial surd. √a + √b and √a − √b are called conjugate surds of each other.

explain.title: Rationalizing a denominator
explain.body: To rationalize a denominator of the form a + b√x or a − b√x, we multiply both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate factor. The product of conjugate surds is a rational number.

mistakes: Changing the sign incorrectly when writing the conjugate; only the sign between the two terms changes.
Multiplying only the denominator by the conjugate instead of multiplying both numerator and denominator.
Forgetting that a negative exponent means a reciprocal.
Adding exponents when dividing powers with the same base; subtract the exponents instead.
Stopping before simplifying the rationalized expression to its simplest form.
Treating every irrational number as a surd; the radicand in a surd must be rational.

explain.title: Real numbers in everyday life
explain.body: Real numbers are used in many fields, including science and engineering, medicine and health, environmental science, computer science, navigation and transportation, surveying and architecture, and statistics. In this section, you use them to solve practical problems.

explain.title: Temperature conversions
explain.body: Use the conversion formula that matches the direction of the question: K = °C + 273; °C = 5/9 (F − 32)°; and °F = (9°C)/5 + 32. Substitute the known temperature and calculate.

explain.title: Profit and loss
explain.body: Your textbook defines: “Profit = selling Price − cost price” and “Loss = cost price − selling price”. For a percentage, compare the profit or loss with the cost price: Profit % = (profit/CP × 100) % and Loss % = (loss/CP × 100) %.

explain.title: Sharing profit and simple profit rate
explain.body: To divide a profit in a ratio, add the ratio parts and give each person their fraction of the total profit. For simple profit, your textbook gives Rate = (amount of profit × 100)/(time × principal).

explain.title: Turning words into equations
explain.body: For questions about sums, differences, or ages, assign a variable to each unknown, write an equation for each condition, and solve. Check that the result matches what the question asks for.

Including an exempted amount in the income used to calculate tax.
Giving a person's present age when the question asks for their age six years ago.
Rounding too early or leaving off the unit, such as °F, kelvin, or Rs.

explain.title: Rational and irrational numbers
explain.body: A rational number can be written as a ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator. A number such as √7 is irrational because 7 is not a perfect square. The real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers.

explain.title: Real-number properties
explain.body: Reflexive property means a number equals itself. Symmetric property lets us reverse an equality. Transitive property carries an equality or inequality through a middle value. Trichotomy says that for two real numbers, exactly one of <, =, or > holds.

explain.title: Distributive and associative properties
explain.body: The distributive property connects multiplication and addition, as in a(b + c) = ab + ac. The associative property changes the grouping of addition or multiplication without changing the result.

explain.title: Simplifying radicals and powers
explain.body: For a perfect-power expression under a radical, use the root index to simplify its exponents. For powers with the same base, use exponent rules and factor common powers before cancelling.

explain.title: Forming equations from problems
explain.body: Use a variable to represent an unknown quantity. Consecutive odd integers differ by 2; for a two-bucket problem, represent the larger amount using the stated difference. For simple profit at different rates, calculate each time period separately.

mistakes: Calling √n rational when n is not a perfect square.

Applying a radical to only part of an expression or dividing exponents by the wrong root index.
In a word problem, solving for a variable but not stating what the requested quantities are.
For the changing-rate simple-profit question, using the new rate for all seven years instead of treating the two periods separately.

notes.title: Recognising Rational and Irrational Numbers
notes.answer: A real number is either rational or irrational.
notes.explanation: Real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers. A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. An irrational number cannot be written as a quotient of integers. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational; non-terminating, non-recurring decimals are irrational.
notes.simple: A decimal that ends or repeats is rational. A decimal that goes on forever without repeating is irrational.
examples: 0.25 is a terminating decimal, so it is rational.
0.333... is recurring, so it is rational.
steps: If it does not end, check whether its digits repeat.
A terminating or recurring decimal is rational.
A non-terminating, non-recurring decimal is irrational.

notes.title: Radicals, surds, and rationalizing denominators
notes.answer: For 3/(√5 + √2), multiply the numerator and denominator by √5 − √2.
notes.explanation: A radical is another way to write a root. To simplify radicals, use the laws of radicals and indices. To rationalize a denominator with two terms, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate.
notes.simple: A surd is an irrational root of a rational number. If a denominator has a sum or difference of two terms, use its conjugate to remove the radical from the denominator.
examples: √5 is a surd; √9 is not a surd because it simplifies to 3.
steps: Identify the radical and its index.
Use the laws of radicals and indices to simplify roots and powers.
For a two-term radical denominator, multiply top and bottom by its conjugate.
notes.checkQuestion: What should you multiply by to rationalize 3/(√5 + √2)?
notes.checkAnswer: Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
